Singular Indefinite Subjects

Everybody / Everything / Nobody / Nothing / Somebody / Something / Anybody / Anything
⭐⭐⭐ (37 PYQs)

🎯 Exam Tips & Common Traps

🎯 Exam Tip: SSC loves testing whether you recognize words like "everybody," "someone," "nothing" as singular. Watch for:

  • Verb agreement: Everybody is (not "are")
  • Pronoun agreement: Everyone should bring his (not "their")
  • With "but/except": verb agrees with the subject before the preposition
  • Nothing = things, Nobody = persons — don't mix them!

Core Rule

The subjects Everybody, Everything, Nobody, Nothing, Somebody, Something, Anybody, Anything are always singular. Hence, they always take a singular verb and singular pronouns.

Examples

✓
Everybody is ready to do his work.
Everybody is singular, so use "is" (not "are") and "his" (not "their").
✗
Anybody can do the work if they try
→ Replace with "he tries" because anybody is singular.
✓
Nothing but some books was available.
Here "but" acts as a preposition. The main subject before the preposition is "Nothing" which is singular.
✗
Nothing but some students was present
→ Replace "nothing" with "nobody" because some students are persons. Use "nobody" to indicate persons.
✓
Something is missing.
✓
Some things are missing.
Note: "Some things" is plural, unlike "Something" which is singular.
✓
Everybody who wants cake should pass his plate.
✗
Everyone section of the society is feeling the pinch.
→ Replace "Everyone" with "Every" because "section" is a noun and "everyone" is a pronoun. A noun and pronoun cannot come together — change pronoun to adjective "every".

Question Tag Rules

→
Somebody was present, weren't they?
Somebody/Nobody are used for persons — use plural question tag.
→
Something was present, wasn't it?
Something/Nothing are used for things — use singular question tag.
→
Nobody was present, were they?

2

Each / Every / Either / Neither / Any / None

Understanding quantity determiners
⭐⭐ (11 PYQs)

🎯 Exam Tips & Common Traps

🎯 Exam Tip: "Each," "every," "either," "neither" are always singular. Common traps:

  • Each of the boys is (not "are")
  • Neither of the two is (not "are")
  • "None" can be singular OR plural depending on context
  • "A number of" = plural | "The number of" = singular

Key Distinctions

✓ When to Use
  • Each: 2 or more persons/things (pronoun & adjective)
  • Every: More than 2 only (always adjective)
  • Either: 2 persons/things (positive sentences)
  • Any: More than 2 (positive sentences)
  • Neither: 2 persons/things (negative sentences)
  • None: More than 2 (negative sentences)
✗ Common Mistakes
  • Every of the girls → use "Each" (need pronoun subject)
  • None of the two → use "Neither"
  • Any of the two → use "Either"
  • Neither of three → use "None"

Examples

✓
Each girl was present.
✓
Each of the girls was present.
✓
Every girl was present.
✗
Every of the girls was present.
→ Replace "every" with "each" — we need a subject (noun/pronoun) and "each" can act as pronoun, but "every" is only an adjective.
✓
Each student wishes to complete his work on time.
✓
Each of the students wishes to complete his work.
After "each of", use plural noun (students) but singular verb (wishes).
✗
None of the two students did the work.
→ Replace "None" with "Neither" — "none" is for more than 2, "neither" is for exactly 2.
✗
Mr. Sharma has three sons, neither of them is hardworking.
→ Replace "Neither" with "None" — three sons = more than 2.
✗
Any of the two students will complete the project.
→ Replace "Any" with "Either" — "either" is for 2 persons/things.
✓
None of the pens is working.
✓
Neither of them attended the function, did they?
✓
Please take one of each. (not "every")
✓
You gave me four toys, and none of them works. (negative sentence)

🎯 Exam Tips & Common Traps

🎯 Exam Tip: "Both...and" always takes a plural verb:

  • Both Ravi and Sita are coming. ✓
  • Compare with "Either...or" → proximity rule applies

Core Rule

"Both" can be used as a pronoun and an adjective. With "Both," the verb is always plural. "Both" always pairs with "and" — never with "as well as."

Examples

✓
Both were present. (pronoun)
✓
Both the students were present. (adjective)
✗

Both my brother and my friends love cricket.

4

Proximity Rule (Either-Or / Neither-Nor)

Verb agrees with the nearer subject
— (0 PYQs)

🎯 Exam Tips & Common Traps

🎯 Exam Tip: With "either...or" / "neither...nor," the verb agrees with the nearer subject:

  • Neither the teacher nor the students were (students = plural, nearer)
  • Neither the students nor the teacher was (teacher = singular, nearer)

Core Rule

When two subjects are joined by Either...or / Neither...nor / Not only...but also, the verb agrees with the subject nearer to the verb.

Examples

✗
Neither the colour or the size of the clothes suits me.
→ Replace "or" with "nor" — "neither" always pairs with "nor". By proximity rule, "the size" is nearer (singular), so verb "suits" is singular.
✓
Not only Ram but also his friends were present.
"friends" is nearer to the verb, so use plural "were".
✓
Either the students or the principal agrees to attend.
"principal" is nearer to the verb, so use singular "agrees".
✗
Neither of the scout leaders know how to trap wild animals.
→ Replace "know" with "knows" — "neither" takes a singular verb. Here "or" is correct because it connects phrase to phrase (conjunction).
5

Numerical Words (Hundred / Thousand / Million / Dozen)

Adjective form stays singular; noun form can pluralize
⭐ (9 PYQs)

🎯 Exam Tips & Common Traps

🎯 Exam Tip: "Hundred," "thousand," "million" stay singular when used as adjectives:

  • Five hundred rupees (not "hundreds")
  • Two thousand people (not "thousands")
  • But: Hundreds of people (noun form = plural)

Core Rule

Words like hundred, thousand, million, dozen stay in singular form when preceded by a numeral (acting as adjective). They can be plural when used as a noun (with "of").

Key insight: When a word comes before a noun, it's an adjective — and adjectives don't have plural forms in English.

Examples

✓
She has donated five thousand rupees.
"Rupees" is noun. Words before nouns are adjectives. Adjectives don't pluralize.
✗
She has donated five thousands rupees.
→ Replace "thousands" with "thousand" — can't pluralize an adjective.
✓
She has donated thousands of rupees.
Here "thousands" is a noun (before "of"). Nouns can be pluralized.
✗
She brought two dozens eggs.
→ Replace "dozens" with "dozen" — "dozen" is acting as adjective here.
✓
She bought two dozen eggs.
✓
She bought dozens of eggs.
"Dozens" is a noun here (before "of").
✓
Dozens of eggs were bought.
✗
Two-thousands people were present.
→ Replace "thousands" with "thousand" — acting as adjective before noun.
✓
Thousands of people were present.
Correct — "thousands" is a noun before "of".

6

Until / Unless / If / Whether / That

Conjunctions for time, condition, doubt, and certainty
⭐⭐⭐ (25 PYQs)

🎯 Exam Tips & Common Traps

🎯 Exam Tip: After "unless/until/if/whether," use Simple Present (not "will"):

  • Unless he works hard (not "will work")
  • If it rains, we will stay home (not "will rain")
  • Two future tenses NEVER in one conditional sentence

Key Distinctions

WordFunctionUsage
UntilConjunction & PrepositionFor time
UnlessAlways ConjunctionFor condition
IfConjunctionCondition (no "will") OR doubt ("will" OK)
WhetherConjunctionDoubt / Uncertainty
ThatConjunctionCertainty / Surety

The If + Not = Unless Rule

Important: If + not = Unless. Since "unless" already contains the negative meaning, never use "not" with "unless".

Examples

✓
I will wait until he comes. (conjunction — connects clause to clause)
✓
I will wait until Monday. (preposition — before a noun)
✓
If he comes, I will go. (condition — no "will" after "if")
✓
I don't know if he will come. (doubt — "will" is OK after "if")
✗
If they will come, I will go.
→ Remove "will" — here "if" expresses condition, not doubt.
✓
Unless he works, he will not succeed. (condition)
✗
Unless one are not punctual in one's work.
→ Replace "unless one are not" with "if one is" — "unless" is already negative, so "not" is redundant.
✓
I don't know if / whether he will come. (both correct)
✓
I don't know whether he will come or not. (use "whether" with "or")
"If" cannot be used with "or not".
✓
I have few doubts that he will come.
"few" = almost no doubt = certainty → use "that".
✓
I have a few doubts whether he will come.
"a few" = some doubt = uncertainty → use "whether".

No Double Comparatives & Superlatives

Never use two degrees of comparison together
⭐⭐ (20 PYQs)

🎯 Exam Tips & Common Traps

🎯 Exam Tip: Never combine two comparative/superlative forms — this is a very common SSC trap:

  • more better ✗ → better ✓
  • most best ✗ → best ✓
  • more easier ✗ → easier ✓
  • most easiest ✗ → easiest ✓

Examples

✗
He is more wiser than his brother.
→ Remove "more" — two comparative degrees ("more" + "wiser") cannot come together.
✗
Sachin is capable of doing more better work.
→ Remove "more" — "more" and "better" are both comparative.
✗
She is the most smartest girl in the class.
→ Remove "most" — two superlative degrees cannot come together.
✓
She is the most intelligent girl in the class. (correct — "most" + positive degree)

Special Note

More better ❌ but Much better ✔
Don't use "more" with "better," but "much" is acceptable with comparative forms.
✓
She is feeling much better.

"Comparatively" & "Relatively" Take Positive Degree

These words already imply comparison
— (1 PYQs)

🎯 Exam Tips & Common Traps

🎯 Exam Tip: Words like "comparatively," "relatively," "fairly," "rather" already imply comparison — use positive degree after them:

  • Comparatively good (not "better")
  • Relatively easy (not "easier")

Core Rule

The words "comparatively" and "relatively" already express comparison within themselves. Therefore, they take adjectives of POSITIVE degree (not comparative).

Examples

✓
The weather is comparatively hot. (not "hotter")
✓
The train is relatively slow. (not "slower")
✓
Earlier job opportunities were comparatively good. (not "better")
✓
It does more harm than good. (not "better" — positive degree before "than")

Explanation: (a) comparatively better ‘Better’ is the comparative degree of ‘good’. The use of ‘comparatively’ with ‘better’ is superfluous, so it will be removed. Hence, ‘better’ is the most appropriate answer. (Correct)
9

"As...As" Construction & Twice/Thrice

Twice/thrice/two times require "as...as" (not comparative)
⭐⭐ (18 PYQs)

🎯 Exam Tips & Common Traps

🎯 Exam Tip: "Twice," "thrice," "two times" require "as...as" (not comparative):

  • He is twice as tall as me ✓
  • He is twice taller than me ✗
  • Structure: twice/thrice + as + adj + as

Core Rule

When sentences contain twice, thrice, two times, etc., use the "as...as" construction. When "as...as" is used for comparison, positive degree comes between them.

Examples

✗
He is twice taller than his brother.
→ Replace "taller than" with "as tall as".
✗
He is two times taller than his brother.
→ Replace "taller than" with "as tall as".
✓
He is two times as tall as his brother.
✗
He is equally as smart as his brother.
→ Remove "equally" — both "equally" and "as...as" express comparison; using both is redundant.
✗
How many eggs and how many money do you need?
→ Replace second "how many" with "how much" — "egg" is countable, "money" is uncountable. Use "many" with countable, "much" with uncountable.
✗
These all mangoes are ripe.
→ Replace "these all" with "all these" — "this/that/these/those" are demonstrative adjectives and come after "all".

Comparing Two Qualities of the Same Person

Use "more" (not "-er") when comparing qualities of one subject
— (3 PYQs)

🎯 Exam Tips & Common Traps

🎯 Exam Tip: When comparing two qualities of the same person/thing, use "more" (not "-er"):

  • She is more beautiful than intelligent ✓
  • She is beautifuller than intelligent ✗

Core Rule

When two qualities of the same person/thing are compared, use "more" (not the "-er" suffix) to form the comparative degree.

Examples

✓
She is smarter than her sister. (comparing two different people — correct)
✗
She is smarter than beautiful.
→ Replace "smarter" with "more smart" — comparing two qualities of the same person.
✓
He is braver than his brother. (comparing two people — correct)
✗
He is braver than wise.
→ Replace "braver" with "more brave" — comparing two qualities of the same person.
📝

Explanation: (d) as more intelligent as ‘As + adjective/adverb + as’ is a comparative structure in which the adjective or the adverb is always in the positive degree. Therefore, ‘more’ will be replaced with ‘much’. Hence, ‘as much intelligent as’ is the most appropriate answer. (Correct)

Main Subject vs Qualifier

Verb agrees with the main subject, not the qualifier
⭐ (7 PYQs)

🎯 Exam Tips & Common Traps

🎯 Exam Tip: Phrases like "as well as," "together with," "along with" do NOT make the subject plural:

  • Ravi, as well as his friends, is coming ✓
  • The captain, along with players, was there ✓
  • Only "and" truly joins subjects into plural

Core Rule

Ensure the verb agrees with the main subject (not the qualifier). Use the preposition "of" to identify: the subject before the preposition is the main subject; the subject after the preposition is the qualifier/object.

Trick: In "X of Y", X = main subject, Y = qualifier. The verb matches X.

Examples

✓
The box of Nestle's chocolates is missing. (box = singular)
✓
The boxes of Nestle's chocolates are missing. (boxes = plural)
✓
The decoration of the rooms is beautiful. (decoration = singular)
✗
A flock of birds were flying over the lake.
→ Replace "were" with "was" — "a flock" is singular.
✗
The prices of tomatoes has soared up to Rs. 65-70.
→ Replace "has" with "have" — "prices" is the main subject (plural).
✗
A letter of recommendation from the principal and HOD have helped him.
→ Replace "have" with "has" — main subject is "a letter" (singular).
✓
One-third of the pillar has rotted away. (pillar = singular)
✓
One-third of the pillars have rotted away. (pillars = plural)
✓
Two-thirds of the pillar has rotted away. (pillar = singular)
✗
Two-third of the pillar has rotted away.
→ Replace "two-third" with "two-thirds" — with "two" we use the plural form "thirds".
✗
A third of us feels compelled to check our phones.
→ Replace "feels" with "feel" — main subject is "us" (plural).

Many / A Number / Many A — Agreement Table

Subject-Verb agreement with special quantifiers
⭐⭐ (20 PYQs)

🎯 Exam Tips & Common Traps

🎯 Exam Tip: Watch the critical difference:

  • Many a student is → singular verb! (despite "many")
  • A number of students are → plural ("a number of" = several)
  • The number of students is → singular ("the number" = the count)

Agreement Table

SubjectNounVerb
Many / A numberPluralPlural
A manyPluralPlural
Many aSingularSingular
The numberPluralSingular
More than oneSingularSingular
More than twoPluralPlural

Examples

✓
Many a girl goes to college in time. (singular noun + singular verb)
✓
A good many girls go to college in time. (plural noun + plural verb)
✗
Many a man have come to India from Canada.
→ Replace "have" with "has" — "many a" takes singular verb.
✗
A great many student have been declared successful.
→ Replace "student" with "students" — after "many" the noun should be plural (verb "have" is plural).
✓
More than one room is vacant. (singular noun + singular verb)
✓
More than two rooms are vacant. (plural noun + plural verb)
✓
More rooms than one are vacant. (plural noun + plural verb)
✓
The number of orders is small. ("the number" = singular verb)
✓
The number of students was low. (plural noun, but singular verb)

Relative Pronoun Agreement (Who / That)

Verb agrees with the antecedent before the relative pronoun
⭐⭐⭐ (42 PYQs)

🎯 Exam Tips & Common Traps

🎯 Exam Tip: The verb after "who/that/which" agrees with the antecedent (the word before):

  • He is one of those students who work hard (students = plural)
  • He is the only one of those students who works hard (one = singular)
  • The phrase "of those students" is just a qualifier — don't let it confuse you!

Core Rule

When a sentence has a relative pronoun (who/that/which), its subject is the word immediately before the relative pronoun (the antecedent). The verb agrees with that antecedent.

Exception: When "only" precedes "one" — "only one" makes it singular.

Examples

✓
Mr. Sharma is one of our officers who are always alert.
"who" refers to "officers" (plural) → plural verb "are".
✓
Mr. Sharma is only one of our officers that is always alert.
"only one" = singular → singular verb "is".
✓
Mr. Sharma is one of our only officers that are always alert.
"only officers" = plural sense → plural verb "are".
✓
It is I who am responsible for the mistake.
"who" refers to "I" (singular) → "am".
✓
He is one of the best writers that have ever lived.
"that" refers to "writers" (plural) → "have".

14

Conditional Sentences

No two future/modal tenses in one conditional sentence
⭐⭐⭐ (28 PYQs)

🎯 Exam Tips & Common Traps

🎯 Exam Tip: In conditional sentences, never use "will" in the if-clause:

  • If he comes, I will go ✓ (not "will come")
  • If I were rich, I would travel (unreal — use "were" for all persons)
  • Had I known, I would have come (past unreal — inverted form)
  • Zero conditional: If + Present, Present (general truths)

Three Types of Conditionals

Conditional Sentence Structure
TypeIf ClauseMain ClauseExample
Type 1Simple PresentSimple FutureIf he comes, I will go.
Type 2Simple PastSimple PastIf he came, I would go.
Type 3Past PerfectWould Have + V3If he had come, I would have gone.
Key Rule: Never use "would have" in the if-clause. Similarly, you cannot have two "will" or two "would" in one conditional sentence.

Examples

✗
If he would have read the instructions carefully, he would not have committed mistakes.
→ Replace "would have read" with "had read" — the if-clause must use Past Perfect (not "would have").
✗
If we had Mohan in our team, we would have won the match.
→ Add "had" after "we" → "If we had had Mohan" — the second part is "would have" (past perfect), so the first part must also be past perfect.

Time Reference vs Action Reference

Time = Simple Past | Action = Perfect Tense
⭐⭐ (21 PYQs)

🎯 Exam Tips & Common Traps

🎯 Exam Tip: Distinguish between time reference and action reference:

  • Time = Simple Past: Before 2020, he lived in Delhi
  • Action = Past Perfect: Before he had finished, the bell rang
  • "After" + action → Past Perfect in the clause before "after"

Core Rule

If a sentence adds a time reference (yesterday, last night, ago), use Simple Past. If it adds an action reference (without specific time), use Present Perfect / Past Perfect.

Examples

✗
He has left for London last night.
→ Replace "has left" with "left" — "last night" is a time reference → Simple Past.
✓
He has left for London. (action reference → Present Perfect)
✗
She had seen the movie yesterday.
→ Replace "had seen" with "saw" — "yesterday" is time reference.
✗
Two years ago, the earthquake had destroyed the city.
→ Replace "had destroyed" with "destroyed" — "two years ago" is time reference.
✗
I was hearing the dog barking last evening.
→ Replace "was hearing" with "heard" — "last evening" is time reference.
✗
Newton has discovered that the force of gravitation makes apples fall.
→ Replace "has discovered" with "discovered" — general fact, not a recent action.
✓
I have taken my lunch. (action reference → Present Perfect)
✗
I have taken my lunch an hour ago.
→ Replace "have taken" with "took" — "an hour ago" is time reference.
📝

Suppositional Sentences (I Wish / As If / As Though)

Unfulfilled wishes take Simple Past with "were"
⭐ (5 PYQs)

🎯 Exam Tips & Common Traps

🎯 Exam Tip: After "wish," "as if," "as though," "if only" — use Simple Past for present unreal:

  • I wish I were taller (not "was" in formal English)
  • He talks as if he knew everything (not "knows")
  • Past unreal: I wish I had studied (Past Perfect)

Core Rule

Sentences with "I wish," "He/She wishes," "as if," "as though" indicating an unfulfilled wish or desire take Simple Past tense. Always use "were" (plural form) for all subjects, including singular ones.

Examples

✓
I wish I were a doctor. (not "was")
✓
If she were a bird, she would fly.
✓
He behaves as if he knew everything. (not "knows")
✓
He commands as though he were my boss. (not "was")
📝

Explanation: (a) were taller The phrase “I wish” is used in the subjunctive mood to express desires. The correct structure is “I wish + simple past.” Therefore, the correct sentence should be “I wish I were taller.” (Correct)

Explanation: (a) were taller The phrase “I wish” is used in the subjunctive mood to express desires. The correct structure is “I wish + simple past.” Therefore, the correct sentence should be “I wish I were taller.” (Correct)

Nouns Joined by Prepositions

Both nouns singular, verb singular — nouns must be the same word
— (0 PYQs)

🎯 Exam Tips & Common Traps

🎯 Exam Tip: When two singular nouns are joined by prepositions, the verb is singular:

  • The quality of the products is good (not "are")
  • Each boy and each girl is present

Examples

✗
Women after women spoke against the cruel practices of dowry.
→ Replace with "Woman after woman" — both nouns should be singular.
✗
Days by days, he is becoming weaker.
→ Replace with "Day by day".
✓
Pile on pile of books was arranged.
✓
Page after page of the Gita was read.
✗
He enquired from doors to doors.
→ Replace with "door to door".
19

Apostrophe with "Else"

's goes on "else" when preceded by somebody/anyone/etc.
— (1 PYQs)

🎯 Exam Tips & Common Traps

🎯 Exam Tip: With words ending in "else," the 's goes on "else":

  • Someone else's bag ✓
  • Someone's else bag ✗
  • Same rule: anybody else's, everybody else's, nobody else's

Core Rule

When pronouns like somebody, anybody, everyone, something are followed by "else", the apostrophe 's is placed on "else" (not on the pronoun).

Note: Two apostrophes cannot come together in a sentence. If two possessives are needed, restructure: "Ram's uncle's friend" → "Friend of Ram's uncle."

Examples

✓
Somebody else's purse has been stolen.
✗
Somebody's else purse has been stolen.
→ Apostrophe goes on "else" → "Somebody else's".

(a) submitted ✓
(b) had submitted
(c) submits

Explanation: (a) submitted The phrase "would rather + subject + verb" is used to express a preference for someone else's action. When referring to a preference for the present or future, simple past tense(V ) is 2 used after the subject. Hence, ‘submitted(V )’ is the most 2 appropriate answer. (Correct)
20

Separate vs Joint Possession

Separate = separate apostrophes | Joint = apostrophe on last noun only
— (0 PYQs)

🎯 Exam Tips & Common Traps

🎯 Exam Tip:

  • Separate possession: Ravi's and Sita's rooms (two separate rooms)
  • Joint possession: Ravi and Sita's room (one shared room)
  • Key: count the apostrophes!

Core Rule

When two nouns joined by "and" have separate possession, each gets its own apostrophe. When they have joint possession, only the last noun gets the apostrophe.

Examples

✗
I went to Ram's and Sita's house and found the couple missing.
→ Replace "Ram's" with "Ram" — they live together (joint possession), so apostrophe only on last noun → "Ram and Sita's house".
✓
Mala's and Priya's account. (separate accounts)
✗
Mala's and Priya's joint account.
→ Replace "Mala's" with "Mala" — it's a joint account → "Mala and Priya's joint account".
21

"One and a Half" Agreement

Plural noun + plural verb | "A ... and a half" = singular
— (0 PYQs)

🎯 Exam Tips & Common Traps

🎯 Exam Tip: "One and a half" takes plural noun + plural verb:

  • One and a half months have passed ✓
  • A month and a half has passed ✓ (singular — "a...and a half")

Examples

✗
One and a half hour.
→ Use "hours" (plural) — "one and a half" takes plural noun.
✓
One and a half hours.
✓
An hour and a half. (singular noun + singular)
✓
One and a half years were wasted. (plural verb)
✓
A year and a half was wasted. (singular verb)
22

Compound Noun Plurals

Add s/es to the ROOT word, not the last word
— (3 PYQs)

🎯 Exam Tips & Common Traps

🎯 Exam Tip: Pluralize the root word in compound nouns:

  • Mothers-in-law ✓ (not "mother-in-laws")
  • Commanders-in-chief ✓
  • Passers-by ✓
  • Rule: the main word gets the plural, not the last word

Plural Forms Table

SingularPlural
Son-in-lawSons-in-law
Brother-in-lawBrothers-in-law
Commander-in-chiefCommanders-in-chief
Passer-byPassers-by
Maid-servantMaid-servants
SpoonfulSpoonfuls
Member of ParliamentMembers of Parliament
Chief MinisterChief Ministers
Girl studentGirl students
Man athleteMen athletes
Woman athleteWomen athletes
Man servantMen servants
Man-of-warMen-of-war

Special Cases

✓
Haves and have-nots. (not "haves not")
✓
Whereabouts (always plural — no singular form)
✗
All his sister-in-laws are married.
→ Replace with "sisters-in-law" — plural goes on root word "sister".

Possession with Compound Nouns

For plural compound nouns, add "s" to the root word. For possession, add apostrophe to the last word.

✗
The commander's-in-chief orders arrived late.
→ Replace with "commander-in-chief's" — apostrophe on last word for possession.
✗
I attended my sister's-in-law marriage yesterday.
→ Replace with "sister-in-law's".

"Cousin" & Redundant Words

Don't add brother/sister after cousin when gender is clear
— (1 PYQs)

🎯 Exam Tips & Common Traps

🎯 Exam Tip: Avoid redundant words — SSC loves testing these:

  • cousin brother ✗ → cousin ✓
  • return back ✗ → return ✓
  • revert back ✗ → revert ✓
  • free gift ✗ → gift ✓
  • advance planning ✗ → planning ✓

Cousin Rule

✗
He is my cousin brother.
→ Remove "brother" — "He" already indicates male gender.
✗
She is my cousin sister.
→ Remove "sister" — "She" already indicates female gender.
✓
I went to the temple with my cousin sister. (gender not clear from context)

Removing Redundant Words

Two nouns with the same meaning cannot come together. Remove the redundant one.

✗
It was a blunder mistake.
→ Remove "mistake" — "blunder" and "mistake" are both nouns with the same meaning.
✗
The angry mob attacked the police officers.
→ Remove "angry" — an angry crowd is already called a "mob".
✗
He is a coward person.
→ Remove "person" — both are nouns with the same meaning.

Common Word Pairs

WrongCorrectReason
passing markspass marks"pass" is the correct adjective form
linking roadlink road"link" is the correct adjective form
put your signput your signatureSign = verb or symbol | Signature = noun (handwriting)
attach your photoattach your photographPhoto = intangible image | Photograph = physical image
pick pocketerpick pocket"pick pocket" is the correct compound noun
bricksbrick"brick" has no plural form
equipmentsequipment"equipment" has no plural (group of tools)
personnelspersonnel"personnel" is already plural

Modal Verbs + V1 (First Form)

Should / Can / Could / May / Might / Will / Shall / Must → always take V1
⭐⭐ (14 PYQs)

🎯 Exam Tips & Common Traps

🎯 Exam Tip: Modal verbs (can, could, may, might, shall, should, will, would, must) are always followed by V1:

  • He can swim ✓ (not "swims" or "swam")
  • She must go ✓
  • Exception: "ought to" — takes "to" + V1
  • "Must have + V3" = past deduction: He must have left

Core Rule

All modal verbs (should, can, could, may, might, will, shall, must, ought to) are always followed by the verb's 1st form (V1) — no "to," no "ing," no past tense.

Examples

✗
You should not boasting of your achievements.
→ Replace "boasting" with "boast" — modal + V1.
✗
The pedestrians should to be cautious.
→ Replace "to be" with "be" — modal + V1 (remove "to").
✗
The conference will been a celebration.
→ Replace "been" with "be" — modal + V1.
✗
We should honest in our dealings.
→ Add "be" after "should" → "should be honest" — when modal is followed by an adjective, add "be".
✗
She must not to waste time.
→ Replace "to waste" with "waste" — modal + V1.
✗
A new chapter may been put forth.
→ Replace "been" with "be" — modal + V1.

Should — Advice vs Condition

Past of "shall" = should (advice) or would (no advice)
— (3 PYQs)

🎯 Exam Tips & Common Traps

🎯 Exam Tip: "Should have + V3" expresses past regret or criticism:

  • You should have told me (but you didn't)
  • He should have been more careful

Core Rules

  • Should can express both advice and condition
  • Past of "shall" = "should" (when giving advice) or "would" (when no advice)
  • Had better = duty/advice, takes V1, present tense meaning

Examples

✓
Should he work, he will succeed. (condition — inverted form)

✓

✓
He said, "We should respect our elders." → They should respect their elders.
Advice → keep "should".
✓
You had better go to school on time. (V1, not "to go" or "gone")
✗
You had better to stop taking medicine.
→ Replace "to stop" with "stop" — "had better" takes V1.

"Used To" — Modal Verb vs Adjective

Modal → V1 | Adjective → Gerund (ing) or Noun
⭐ (5 PYQs)

🎯 Exam Tips & Common Traps

🎯 Exam Tip: Two completely different uses of "used to":

  • Modal verb (past habit): I used to play cricket → V1 after "used to"
  • Adjective (accustomed): I am used to playing → gerund after "used to"
  • Negative: I didn't use to play (modal) | I'm not used to playing (adjective)

Core Rule

"Used to" can function as a modal verb (takes V1) or an adjective (takes gerund -ing form or noun). If there's already a main helping verb (is, was, got), then "used to" is an adjective.

Examples

✓
He used to work hard. (modal verb → V1 "work")
✓
He is used to working hard. (adjective → gerund "working")
"is" is already the main verb, so "used to" is an adjective → takes gerund.
✓
He is used to hard-work. (adjective → noun)
✓
He got used to working hard. (adjective → gerund, "got" is main verb)
✓
Camels are used to carry loads. (passive voice → "used to" is main verb → to + V1)

Redundant Modal Combinations

Can/Could + able | May/Might + possible = redundant
— (0 PYQs)

🎯 Exam Tips & Common Traps

🎯 Exam Tip: Never combine modals with "able/possible" — this is redundant:

  • can able ✗ → can or is able to ✓
  • may possible ✗ → may or is possible ✓
  • will going to ✗ → will or is going to ✓

Core Rule

Can/Could already means ability — don't add "able/capable". May/Might already means possibility — don't add "possible/likely".

Examples

✗
He may possibly attend the party.
→ Remove "possibly" — "may" already expresses possibility.
✗
It may likely rain.
→ Remove "likely" — "may" already expresses possibility.
✗
I can be able to do the work.
→ Remove "be able to" — "can" already means ability.
✗
The students could not be able to attend the meeting.
→ Remove "be able to".
28

"With a View To" & "Looking Forward To"

Both always take Gerunds (ing form)
⭐ (9 PYQs)

🎯 Exam Tips & Common Traps

🎯 Exam Tip: "To" in these phrases is a preposition (not infinitive marker), so it takes a gerund (V-ing):

  • with a view to studying ✓ (not "study")
  • looking forward to meeting ✓
  • accustomed to eating ✓
  • devoted to serving ✓

Core Rule

Both "with a view to" (= with the purpose of) and "looking forward to" (= expect/anticipate something positive) are prepositional phrases that always take a gerund (ing form) — never a bare verb.

Examples

✓

✓

✗

→ Replace "hear" with "hearing" — gerund after "looking forward to".
✗
With a view to avoid traffic accidents, the road was blocked.
→ Replace "avoid" with "avoiding" — gerund after "with a view to".

Gerund vs Participle

Gerund = ...ing as Noun | Participle = Verb as Adjective
— (3 PYQs)

🎯 Exam Tips & Common Traps

🎯 Exam Tip: Know the difference:

  • Gerund (acts as noun): Swimming is good exercise
  • Participle (acts as adjective): The swimming boy fell into the pool
  • Test: Replace with "it" — if it works, it's a gerund

Key Differences

Gerund (ing form as Noun)
  • Acts as subject or object
  • Takes possessive case before it (his, my, your)
  • Swimming is good for health.
  • I don't mind his staying.
Participle (Verb as Adjective)
  • Present Participle: ...ing as adjective
  • Past Participle: V3 as adjective
  • Takes objective case before it (him, me, us)
  • I saw him leaving.

Examples

✓
Swimming is good for health. (gerund = subject)
✓
He enjoys swimming. (gerund = object)
✓
He is fond of swimming. (gerund = object of preposition)
✓
No smoking. (gerund)
✓
The book is interesting. (present participle = adjective)
✓
The broken glasses were repaired. (past participle = adjective)
✓
I don't mind his staying late hours. (gerund → possessive case)
✗
Due to me being a new comer does not excuse your fault.
→ Replace "me" with "my" — "due to" is a prepositional phrase → gerund follows → possessive case before gerund.
✓
I saw him leaving the house. (participle → objective case)
✓
He saw us parking the car. (participle → objective case)
📝

✅ Correct Answer: (c) is playing

Infinitive & Bare Infinitive

Infinitive = to + V1 | Bare Infinitive = V1 without "to"
⭐⭐ (18 PYQs)

🎯 Exam Tips & Common Traps

🎯 Exam Tip: After certain verbs, use bare infinitive (without "to"):

  • Let him go (not "to go")
  • Make him work
  • Had better leave
  • Would rather stay
  • After prepositions → use gerund: insist on going

Bare Infinitive Triggers

Certain verbs/phrases take Bare Infinitive (V1 without "to"):

Make / Made
→ V1
Bid / Bade
→ V1
See / Saw
→ V1
Hear / Heard
→ V1
Let
→ V1
But
→ V1
Than
→ V1
Except
→ V1
Would rather
→ V1
Sooner than
→ V1

Examples

✗
I bade him to do the work.
→ Remove "to" — "bade" takes bare infinitive in active voice.
✓
I was bade to do the work. (passive → to + V1 is OK)
✗
The cruel lady made her servant to do all the chores.
→ Remove "to" — "made" takes bare infinitive.
✓
I was made to do all the work. (passive → to + V1 is OK)
✗
I let him to enter the room.
→ Remove "to" — "let" takes bare infinitive.
✗
He does nothing else but to play.
→ Remove "to" — "but" takes bare infinitive.
✗
I would rather go to school than to stay at home.
→ Remove "to" — "would rather" and "than" both take bare infinitive.
✓
To die with honour is better than to live with dishonour.
Here infinitive (to die) is compared with infinitive (to live) → "to" is used with "than" in comparisons.
✓
I helped her do the work. OR I helped her to do the work. (both OK)
✓
I saw her do the work. (bare infinitive) OR I saw her doing the work. (present participle)
✗
I saw her to do the work.
→ Remove "to" — "saw" takes bare infinitive, not "to + V1".
✓
He couldn't help but shed tears. ("but" → bare infinitive)
✓
He couldn't stop himself from shedding tears. ("from" = preposition → gerund)

Irregular Verb Forms

Critical verb forms that frequently appear in exams
⭐⭐⭐⭐ (54 PYQs)

🎯 Exam Tips & Common Traps

🎯 Exam Tip: Memorize these commonly confused irregular verb forms — very frequently tested:

  • Lie (recline): lie → lay → lain
  • Lie (tell falsehood): lie → lied → lied
  • Lay (put): lay → laid → laid
  • Drink: drink → drank → drunk
  • Shrink: shrink → shrank → shrunk
  • Swim: swim → swam → swum

Confusing Verb Pairs

VerbV1V2V3Meaning
Lie (untruth)LieLiedLiedTo tell a falsehood
Lie (on bed)LieLayLainTo recline
Lay (put)LayLaidLaidTo place something
RiseRiseRoseRisenTo go up (intransitive)
RaiseRaiseRaisedRaisedTo lift something (transitive)
FlyFlyFlewFlownTo move through air
FlowFlowFlowedFlowedTo move like liquid
Hang (prisoner)HangHangedHangedExecution
Hang (clothes)HangHungHungTo suspend
Bear (birth)BearBoreBornTo give birth
Bear (carry)BearBoreBorneTo endure/carry
FindFindFoundFoundTo discover
FoundFoundFoundedFoundedTo establish
FallFallFellFallenTo drop down
Fell (cut)FellFelledFelledTo cut down a tree
WindWindWoundWoundTo twist/turn
Wound (injure)WoundWoundedWoundedTo injure
Bid (auction)BidBidBidTo offer a price
Bid (order)BidBadeBiddenTo command

Irregular Verbs (Same Forms)

Cast
cast — cast — cast
Broadcast
broadcast — broadcast — broadcast
Telecast
telecast — telecast — telecast
Forecast
forecast — forecast — forecast
Spread
spread — spread — spread
Burst
burst — burst — burst
Cost
cost — cost — cost
Cut
cut — cut — cut
Put
put — put — put
Shut
shut — shut — shut

Other Irregular Verbs

V1V2V3
HideHidHidden
BeginBeganBegun
ComeCameCome
RunRanRun
SwimSwamSwum
SlaySlewSlain
HoldHeldHeld
BeatBeatBeaten
BiteBitBitten
BuildBuiltBuilt
SendSentSent
FeelFeltFelt
ShootShotShot
GrindGroundGround

Noun / Verb Pairs

NounVerb
AdviceAdvise
PracticePractise
LicenceLicense
EffectAffect
ComplaintComplain
Avenge (verb)Revenge (noun & verb — takes reflexive pronoun)

Examples

✓
He lay in the shade of the tree. (lie on bed → lay)
✓
He lied to me yesterday. (tell untruth → lied)
✓
The hens have laid eggs. (lay → laid)
✓
The water level rose by two feet. (rise → rose, intransitive)
✓
He raised many questions. (raise → raised, transitive)
✓
The clothes were hung. (suspend → hung)
✓
The prisoner was hanged. (execution → hanged)
✓
Gandhi was born on 2nd October. (birth → born)
✓
He has borne many difficulties in life. (endure → borne)
✓
The birds have flown. (fly → flown)
✓
He raised the flag. (transitive → raised)

32

Separate Auxiliary Verbs for Different Subjects

Different number subjects need separate auxiliaries
⭐⭐ (14 PYQs)

🎯 Exam Tips & Common Traps

🎯 Exam Tip: When two subjects of different number need different auxiliaries, repeat the auxiliary:

  • He is smart and they are smart ✓
  • He is smart and they smart ✗

Core Rule

When two subjects are different (one singular, one plural), each needs its own auxiliary verb. When both subjects are the same number, they can share one auxiliary.

Examples

✗
Two were killed and one injured.
→ Add "was" after "one" — different number subjects need separate auxiliaries.
✗
One was killed and two injured.
→ Add "were" after "two".
✗
He has and will help the poor.
→ Add "helped" after "has" → "He has helped and will help the poor."
✗
His assistants have and are still doing great jobs.
→ Add "done" after "have" → "have done and are still doing."
📝

Stative Verbs vs Action Verbs

Stative → Adjective | Action → Adverb
— (0 PYQs)

🎯 Exam Tips & Common Traps

🎯 Exam Tip: Stative verbs (feel, look, smell, taste, sound) take adjectives (not adverbs):

  • The food tastes good ✓ (not "well")
  • She looks beautiful ✓ (not "beautifully")
  • I feel bad ✓ (not "badly")
  • Exception: "He looks well" = he is in good health

Stative Verbs (take ADJECTIVES)

Stative verbs describe a state or situation, not an action. They take adjectives (not adverbs) after them.

Opinion
believe, know, think, support, disagree
Emotion
like, love, hate, need, want, wish, desire, fear
Senses
look, see, appear, taste, sound, hear, feel, seem, smell
Possession
have, own, possess, belong, control
Condition
weigh, lack, involve, resemble, include

Action Verbs (take ADVERBS)

Action verbs express a physical or mental action. They take adverbs after them.

Physical
run, walk, jump, eat, drink, cry, skip, pull, push
Mental
talk, sing, speak, study, teach, try, bring, make, bake

Examples

✓
The birds sang sweetly. (action verb → adverb)
✓
The food tasted sweet. (stative verb → adjective)
✓
She looks beautiful. (stative → adjective)
✓
She ate all the food hungrily. (action → adverb)
✗
He is being very politely.
→ Replace "politely" with "polite" — "being" is stative → adjective.
✗
Mangoes taste more sweetly than any other fruit.
→ Replace "more sweetly" with "sweeter" — "taste" is stative → adjective.
✓
The flowers smell so sweet. (stative → adjective)
✗
The old man is blindly.
→ Replace "blindly" with "blind" — "is" is stative → adjective.

Special Stative Verb Rules

Important: Stative verbs do NOT take "-ing" form in their normal meaning. "Have" (possession), "see" (perception), "believe," "think," "remember," "belong" — none of these form "-ing" in their stative sense.
✓
He is having a meeting tomorrow. ✔ (having = arranged meeting, not possession)
✓
I am having dinner. ✔ (having = eating, not possession)
✗
He is seeing the movie.
→ Replace "seeing" with "watching" — "see" (perception) doesn't take "-ing".
✓
He is seeing the PM tomorrow. ✔ (seeing = meeting, not perception)
✓
Seeing is believing. ✔ (both are gerunds here)
✗
Every year our association is having a meeting.
→ Replace "is having" with "has" — habitual action → Simple Present.
✗
I think our furniture needing to be polished.
→ Replace "needing" with "needs" — "need" is stative, no "-ing". "Furniture" is singular → "needs".
✗
I can't go out as I am not having an umbrella.
→ Replace with "don't have" — "have" (possession) doesn't take "-ing".
✗
I am thinking you were aware of the rules.
→ Replace "am thinking" with "think" — general statement → Simple Present.
✗
Some people are believing that women cannot compete.
→ Replace "are believing" with "believe" — general statement → Simple Present.
✗
Ramesh smiled when he was remembering his hard early years.
→ Replace "was remembering" with "remembered" — "remember" is stative, no "-ing".
✗
People who are not belonging to any party want to divide the country.
→ Replace "are not belonging" with "do not belong" — "belong" is stative, no "-ing".

Personal Pronoun Rules

Case rules for pronouns joined by and/or, after let, it is, than
— (3 PYQs)

🎯 Exam Tips & Common Traps

🎯 Exam Tip: After "let," "it is," "than" — use the correct pronoun case:

  • Let him go (not "he")
  • It is I (formal) / It is me (informal)
  • He is taller than I (formal — "than I am")

Rule 1: Same Case with "And" / "Or"

Pronouns joined by "and" or "or" should be in the same case (both subjective or both objective).

✗
These books are for you and I.
→ Replace "I" with "me" — objective case needed after "for".
✓
You and I will do the work. (both subjective)
✗
Ram or myself will do the work.
→ Replace "myself" with "I" — reflexive pronoun cannot be a subject.
✗
There is an understanding between Ram and I.
→ Replace "I" with "me" — objective case after "between".

Rule 2: After "Let" → Objective Case

✓
Let him do the work. (objective case)
✓
Let us attend the meeting.
✗
The principal ordered to let Ram and I enter.
→ Replace "I" with "me" — after "let" use objective case.

Rule 3: After "It is" / "It was" → Subjective Case

✓
It was he who helped me. (not "him")
✓
It is I who am responsible. (not "me")

Rule 4: After "Than" → Depends on Meaning

✓
I know better than he. (subject comparison: I vs he)
✓
I know you better than him. (object comparison: you vs him)
✓
I know you better than he. (subject comparison: he knows you)
Both "him" and "he" are correct after "than" — the meaning changes.

Who vs Whom

Who = subject (nominative) | Whom = object (accusative)
⭐⭐⭐ (27 PYQs)

🎯 Exam Tips & Common Traps

🎯 Exam Tip: Quick test — replace with he/she (who) or him/her (whom):

  • Who/Whom did you meet? → "I met him" → Whom
  • Who/Whom is there? → "He is there" → Who
  • After preposition: To whom did you give it?

Core Rule

Who is used for the subject. Whom is used for the object. After a preposition, always use whom.

Examples

✓
A scientist who won two Nobel prizes. (subject of "won")
✓
The person who helped him is my friend. (subject of "helped")
✓
I will visit my parents who live in Delhi. (subject of "live")
✓
The person to whom I am speaking is my friend. (after preposition "to")
✓
By whom was the Ramayana written?
✓
The person whom I met yesterday is my friend. (object of "met")
✓
The person who met me yesterday is my friend. (subject of "met")
✓
He is the person who, everyone thought, has stolen the purse. (subject of "has stolen")
✓
I know the boy who they say has stolen the purse. (subject of "has stolen")

Pronoun Agreement with Compound Subjects

With/along with → first subject | Or/nor → nearer subject
⭐ (5 PYQs)

🎯 Exam Tips & Common Traps

🎯 Exam Tip: "With/along with/as well as" — pronoun agrees with the first subject:

  • Ravi with his friends is here — he (not "they")

Core Rule

  • With / along with / except / as well as / together with / besides → verb and pronoun according to FIRST subject
  • Or / either-or / neither-nor / not only-but also → verb and pronoun according to NEARER subject

Examples

✓
The students as well as the teacher did their work. (their = students)
✓
He was one of those students who completed their project. (who = students)
✓
Neither Ram nor his friends brought their documents. (their = friends, nearer)
✓
The treasurer and secretary gave his consent. (one person with two roles → his)
✓
The treasurer and the secretary gave their consent. (two different people → their)
✓
He was only one of the students who completed his work. (only one → singular)
✓
Everybody should respect his elders. (singular)
✓
All should do their work. (plural)
✓
Nobody was ready to leave his seat. (singular)

Pronoun Arrangement Order

Normal: 231 | Confessional: 123 | Plural: 123
— (1 PYQs)

🎯 Exam Tips & Common Traps

🎯 Exam Tip: Pronoun order: 2nd →3rd →1st (you, he, I):

  • You, he and I ✓ (normal order)
  • I, you and he ✗ (wrong order)
  • Exception (confession/fault): I, you and he ✓

Arrangement Diagram

Normal Sentence
2nd → 3rd → 1st
You, he and I
Negative / Confessional
1st → 2nd → 3rd
I, you and he
Plural Pronouns
1st → 2nd → 3rd
We, you and they

Two-Person Combinations

CombinationOrderExample
1st + 2nd21You and I will complete our work.
2nd + 3rd23You and he will complete your work.
1st + 3rd31Priya and I will complete our work.

Examples

✓
I, you and he → You, he and I are responsible. (231 — normal)
✓
You, he and I → I, you and he are responsible. (123 — confessional)
✓
We, you and they are ready. (123 — plural)
✓
Ram and I are friends. (1st + 3rd → 31: "Ram" is 3rd person)
✓
Ram or I am friends. (verb agrees with nearer subject "I")

🎯 Exam Tips & Common Traps

🎯 Exam Tip:

  • Very + positive degree / present participle: very good, very interesting
  • Much + comparative / past participle: much better, much tired
  • Very much is correct (not "much very")
  • "Very" intensifies; "much" shows degree of comparison

Examples

She is very good. (very + positive degree)
✗
She is very better.

She is much smarter. (much + comparative)
✓
He was much shocked. (much + past participle)
✓
The news is very shocking. (very + present participle)

Adverb Position (Frequency)

Before the verb | Between auxiliary and main verb
⭐⭐⭐⭐ (51 PYQs)

🎯 Exam Tips & Common Traps

🎯 Exam Tip: Adverbs of frequency (always, never, often, usually, sometimes) — very frequently tested:

  • Before the main verb: I always wake up early
  • Between auxiliary and main verb: I have always liked it
  • After "be" verb: He is always late
  • Position changes meaning: Only I saw him vs I only saw him

Core Rule

Adverbs of frequency (always, never, seldom, rarely, scarcely, often) go before the verb. When both auxiliary + main verb are present, the adverb goes between them.

Examples

✓
He never helps me. (not "He helps me never")
✓
She is always making noise. (between "is" and "making")

MPT Rule — Manner → Place → Time

When all three adverbs appear together, follow this order
— (0 PYQs)

🎯 Exam Tips & Common Traps

🎯 Exam Tip: When multiple adverbs appear together, follow MPT order:

  • Manner → Place → Time
  • She danced gracefully on the stage yesterday

Order Diagram

MPT Adverb Order
Manner
→
Place
→
Time

Examples

✓
She sang beautifully at the party last night. (Manner → Place → Time)
✗
She sang last night at the party beautifully.
→ Correct order: beautifully → at the party → last night.

Come to my house at 7 o'clock. (Place → Time)
✓
They went to Jaipur last evening. (Place → Time)
✓
He spoke loudly at the meeting yesterday. (Manner → Place → Time)

Placement of "Only"

Place "only" immediately before the word it modifies
— (3 PYQs)

🎯 Exam Tips & Common Traps

🎯 Exam Tip: Place "only" immediately before the word it modifies:

  • Only I saw him = nobody else saw him
  • I only saw him = I didn't talk to him
  • I saw only him = I didn't see anyone else

Examples

✓
Only she can speak. (only = she is the one who can)
✓
She can speak only. (only = speaking is the only thing)
✗
She only answered two questions.
→ "She answered only two questions." — "only" should modify "two".
✗
Only the death of her son made her weep.
→ "The death of her only son made her weep." — "only" should modify "son".
✗
She only eats strawberries.
→ "She eats only strawberries." — "only" should modify "strawberries".
📝

Inversion with Adverbs at Sentence Start

Never, hardly, scarcely, few, little, too, so → subject-verb inversion
⭐⭐ (19 PYQs)

🎯 Exam Tips & Common Traps

🎯 Exam Tip: When these adverbs begin a sentence, invert subject and verb — very frequently tested:

  • Never have I seen such a sight
  • Hardly had she arrived when it rained
  • No sooner had he left than the phone rang
  • Scarcely had they begun when it stopped
  • Pairing: hardly/scarcely + when | no sooner + than

Core Rule

When certain adverbs begin a sentence, the subject and verb are inverted (verb comes before subject). These adverbs include: Never, Not, Few, Little, Hardly, Scarcely, Too, So.

Examples

✗
Never he does help me.
→ "Never does he help me." — inversion when "never" starts the sentence.
✗
Never I have met such a person.
→ "Never have I met such a person."
✓
I have never met such a person. (adverb NOT at start → no inversion)
✗
Hardly he did attend the class.
→ "Hardly did he attend the class."
📝

48

Articles with Proper Nouns / Names

"A" before name = some/any person | "The" = quality comparison
— (0 PYQs)

🎯 Exam Tips & Common Traps

🎯 Exam Tip: Articles with proper nouns:

  • No article: Delhi, India, Ganga (unique names)
  • "The": the Yamuna, the Himalayas, the Sahara
  • "A" before name = "some/any": a Mr. Sharma (some person named Sharma)

Examples

✓
A Mr. Ram has come. (some Mr. Ram, unknown person)
✓
Mr. Ram has come. (specific, known person — no article)
✗
The Newton was great.
→ Can't use "the" directly with a proper noun.
✓
He is the Newton of our class. (quality comparison → "the" is OK)
✓
Kalidas was the Shakespeare of India. (quality comparison)
✓
The judge in him prevailed. (his judging quality, not a real judge)
49

The + Superlative / Ordinal / Comparative

The + superlative | The + ordinal | The + comparative + of (not than)
⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ (148 PYQs)

🎯 Exam Tips & Common Traps

🎯 Exam Tip: Use "the" with — most tested article rule:

  • Superlatives: the best, the most beautiful
  • Ordinals: the first, the second, the last
  • Comparative + "of the two": the better of the two (not "than")
  • "The + comparative, the + comparative": The more you study, the better you become

Examples

✓
He is the best boy. (the + superlative)
✓
The first chapter. (the + ordinal)
✓
He is the better of the two boys. (the + comparative + of)
✗
He is the better than the two boys.
→ Remove "the" → "He is better than the two boys." OR use "the better of".

Parallel Structure (The...the...)

✓
The higher you go, the cooler you feel.
✓
Greater the demand, the higher the price.

50

Single Unit — Article Before First Subject Only

When two things form one unit, article goes only before the first
— (0 PYQs)

🎯 Exam Tips & Common Traps

🎯 Exam Tip: When two nouns form one unit, article goes only before the first:

  • Bread and butter is my breakfast (no article before "butter")
  • A cup and saucer (not "a cup and a saucer")

Examples

✓
A cup and saucer (one unit — article before first only)
✗
A cup and a saucer (implies two separate items)
✓
A singer and scientist (one person who is both)
✗
A singer and a scientist (two different people)
51

General vs Particular — Article Usage

General sense = no article | Particular/specific = use article
⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ (222 PYQs)

🎯 Exam Tips & Common Traps

🎯 Exam Tip: — second most tested article rule:

  • General = no article: Life is short (life in general)
  • Particular = use article: the life of a soldier (specific life)
  • Man is mortal (general) vs The man is tall (specific)
  • Gold is precious (general) vs The gold in this ring (specific)

Examples

✓
Man is mortal. (general mankind — no article)
✓
I saw the man in the forest. (specific man — with article)
✓
Water is essential. (general — no article)
✓
The water of the river is dirty. (specific — with article)
✓
Gold is precious. (general — no article)
✓
The gold of this ring is inferior. (specific — with article)

Language & Nationality — Article Rules

No article before language names | "The + nationality" = people
— (0 PYQs)

🎯 Exam Tips & Common Traps

🎯 Exam Tip:

  • No article before languages: I speak Hindi
  • "The + nationality" = the people: The Indians are hardworking
  • No article before meals: breakfast, lunch, dinner
  • No article before games/sports: cricket, football

Examples

✓
He studied English. (language — no article)
✗
He studied the English.
✓
The English defeated the French. (the people — with article)
✗
The French is spoken by the French.
→ Remove "the" from first "French" — first = language (no article), second = people (with article).
54

Since vs For

Since = point of time | For = duration (length of time)
⭐⭐⭐ (27 PYQs)

🎯 Exam Tips & Common Traps

🎯 Exam Tip:

  • Since = point of time: since 2020, since Monday, since morning
  • For = duration: for two years, for a long time
  • Present Perfect with both: I have lived here since 2020 / for five years
  • "Since" can also be a conjunction: Since he left, I have been sad

Key Distinctions

Since (Point of Time)
  • Used with perfect and perfect continuous tenses
  • since January, since Monday, since 2014
  • since childhood, since infancy (stages of life)
  • since ancient/medieval/modern times
  • since time immemorial
For (Duration)
  • Used with all three perfect tenses
  • for a month, for a year, for two days
  • for a week, for a long time
  • Can be used with simple tenses too

Important Notes

"Since" + not with plurals: "since last two weeks" ❌ → "for last two weeks" ✔
Stage of life (childhood, infancy) → use since. Ancient/Medieval/Modern Times → use since.

Transitive Verbs Don't Take Prepositions

But their noun forms DO take prepositions

🎯 Exam Tips & Common Traps

🎯 Exam Tip: Some verbs are transitive (no preposition needed) — SSC loves testing these:

  • discuss about ✗ → discuss ✓
  • enter into ✗ → enter ✓
  • reach to ✗ → reach ✓
  • attack on ✗ → attack ✓
  • emphasize on ✗ → emphasize ✓

Examples

✓

✓
An attack on the boy. (noun — preposition needed)
✓
He ordered coffee. (verb — no preposition)
✓
An order for coffee. (noun — preposition needed)
✓
He emphasized the point. (verb — no preposition)
✓
Put emphasis on the point. (noun — preposition needed)
✓
Despite hard work. (no "of")
✓
In spite of hard work. (has "of" — different phrase)
✓
He investigated the matter. (no "into")
✓
He entered into an alliance. (not a place → preposition OK)
✓
He violated the rules. (no "against")
✓
He invaded the territory. (no "on")
✓
He resembled his parents. (no "to")

Between vs Among

Between = 2 (or distinct items) | Among = more than 2 (as a group)
⭐⭐ (15 PYQs)

🎯 Exam Tips & Common Traps

🎯 Exam Tip:

  • Between = 2 persons/things (or distinct individual items): between you and me
  • Among = more than 2 (as a group): among the students
  • Tricky: Between the five of us ✓ (distinct individuals, not a group)

Core Rule

Between is for 2 things (or more if they are separate/distinct). Among is for more than 2 (as a group). "Between" is never followed by "and" with "among."

Words always followed by "between": distinguish, differentiate, connection, difference, link, relationship, choose, divide.

Examples

✓
Between the two cats. (2 things)
✓
Among the students. (more than 2, as a group)
✓
Between England, America and Russia. (distinct nations — "between" is OK)
✓
Choose between the singers. (not "among")
✓
Difference between the brothers. (not "among")
✓
Divide the property between the members. (not "among")

In vs Into

In = no change of state | Into = change of state | Enter + place = no preposition
⭐⭐⭐ (31 PYQs)

🎯 Exam Tips & Common Traps

🎯 Exam Tip:

  • In = static (no movement): He is in the room
  • Into = movement/change: He walked into the room
  • Enter = "go into" → no preposition after "enter"
  • Convert into = change form | Convert to = change religion/belief

Core Rules

  • In = already inside (no change of medium/state)
  • Into = entering (change of medium/state)
  • Enter + place = NO preposition needed
  • Throw + in (not "into")

Examples

✓
He dived into the river. (change — entering from outside)
✓
He was swimming in the river. (already inside)
✓
Students walked into the room. (entering from outside)
✓
Frog was lying in the well. Frog jumped into the well.
✓
Water was in the bottle. He poured water into the bottle.
✓
Translate the passage into English.
✓
Translate from Hindi to English. (from...to — not "into")
✓
He entered the classroom. (no preposition)
✗
He entered in/into the classroom.
→ Remove "in/into" — "enter" + place takes no preposition.
✓
He entered into an alliance / agreement / discussion. (not a place → preposition OK)
✓
He threw the paper in the dustbin. (throw + in, not "into")

Of vs Off

Of = possession/cause/material | Off = separation/detachment
⭐⭐⭐ (36 PYQs)

🎯 Exam Tips & Common Traps

🎯 Exam Tip:

  • Of = possession, cause, material: the roof of the house
  • Off = separation, detachment: He fell off the ladder
  • Cure of = remedy | Cure for = treatment

Uses of "Of"

  • Possession/ownership: The dramas of Shakespeare
  • Cause/reason: He died of cancer
  • Origin: The water of the Ganga
  • Material: A necklace made of gold
  • Choice/selection: One of the students

Death Expressions (Fixed Prepositions)

ExpressionContext
Died ofDisease (malaria, cancer)
Died inAccident, riots
Died fromInjury, over-eating, wound
Died ofStarvation, thirst (hunger)
Died withGrief, shame, sorrow
Died byViolence
Died forCountry (sacrifice)

Uses of "Off"

Off = separation / detachment

✓
Switch off the fan. (not "of")
✓
The wheel came off the cart.
✓
The plane took off.
✗
Put off the candle.
→ "Put off" means postpone. Use "Put out" = extinguish.

Verbs with "Of"

These verbs always take "of": dispose, rid, rob, acquit, shortage, deprive, guilty, accused, keep clear, lack, devoid.

Exception: "Dispense" takes "with". "Vex with a person" but "Vex at a thing."

Direct & Indirect Speech (Narration)

Rules for converting direct speech to reported speech
⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ (238 PYQs)

Core Rule

Direct Speech quotes the exact words spoken. Indirect (Reported) Speech reports what was said without quoting word-for-word. When converting from direct to indirect speech, you must change pronouns, tenses, and time/place references.

Tense Change Rules (Backshift)

→
Simple Present → Simple Past
Direct: He said, "I play cricket."
Indirect: He said that he played cricket.
→
Present Continuous → Past Continuous
Direct: She said, "I am reading a book."
Indirect: She said that she was reading a book.
→
Present Perfect → Past Perfect
Direct: He said, "I have finished."
Indirect: He said that he had finished.
→
Simple Past → Past Perfect
Direct: She said, "I visited the museum."
Indirect: She said that she had visited the museum.
→
Will → Would | Can → Could | May → Might
Direct: He said, "I will come."
Indirect: He said that he would come.

Pronoun & Reference Changes

✓
This → that | These → those | Here → there | Now → then
✓
Today → that day | Yesterday → the previous day | Tomorrow → the next/following day
✓
Ago → before | Last night → the previous night | Last week → the previous week

Reporting Verb Patterns

✓
Statements: said / told + that
"I am happy." → He said that he was happy. / He told me that he was happy.
✓
Yes/No Questions: asked + if / whether
"Are you coming?" → She asked if I was coming.
✓
Wh-Questions: asked + wh-word (no inversion in indirect)
"Where do you live?" → He asked where I lived.
✓
Commands: told / ordered / advised + to + V1
"Open the door." → He told me to open the door.
✓
Requests: requested / begged + to + V1
"Please help me." → She requested me to help her.
✓
Exclamations: exclaimed with + emotion + that
"What a beautiful day!" → He exclaimed with joy that it was a beautiful day.

Common Mistakes

✗
He asked me that where I lived.
→ Don't use "that" with wh-questions. Use: He asked me where I lived.
✗
She said me that she was tired.
→ "Say" doesn't take an indirect object. Use: She told me that she was tired. OR She said that she was tired.
✗
He told that he will come.
→ Backshift the tense: He told me that he would come.

🎯 Exam Tips & Common Traps

🎯 Exam Tip: Key rules for Direct → Indirect Speech conversion:

  • Present → Past | Past → Past Perfect | Will → Would
  • "This" → "that" | "These" → "those" | "Here" → "there"
  • "Now" → "then" | "Today" → "that day" | "Yesterday" → "the previous day"
  • Questions: use "asked" + if/whether (yes/no) or wh-word
  • Commands: use "told/ordered/advised" + to + V1
  • Exclamations: use "exclaimed with joy/sorrow/surprise" + that
📝

(a) She asked them if they would be attending the conference. ✓

Active & Passive Voice

Converting between active and passive voice forms
⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ (250 PYQs)

Core Rule

In Active Voice, the subject performs the action. In Passive Voice, the subject receives the action. Conversion: Object → Subject, Verb → be + V3, Subject → by + object. Only transitive verbs can be passive.

Tense-wise Passive Formation

→
Simple Present: am/is/are + V3
Active: She writes a letter. → Passive: A letter is written by her.
→
Simple Past: was/were + V3
Active: He ate the cake. → Passive: The cake was eaten by him.
→
Present Continuous: am/is/are + being + V3
Active: They are building a house. → Passive: A house is being built by them.
→
Past Continuous: was/were + being + V3
Active: She was cooking food. → Passive: Food was being cooked by her.
→
Present Perfect: has/have + been + V3
Active: He has completed the work. → Passive: The work has been completed by him.
→
Past Perfect: had + been + V3
Active: She had finished the task. → Passive: The task had been finished by her.
→
Future Simple: will/shall + be + V3
Active: They will deliver the package. → Passive: The package will be delivered by them.
→
Modal Verbs: modal + be + V3
Active: You must submit the form. → Passive: The form must be submitted by you.

Special Passive Constructions

✓
Two objects: Either can become subject
He gave me a book. → I was given a book. OR A book was given to me.
✓
Imperatives: Let + object + be + V3
Open the door. → Let the door be opened.

No Passive Voice For

✗
Intransitive verbs: go, come, die, sleep, arrive, fall, rise, happen
→ "He died" cannot become passive — "die" has no object.
✗
Stative verbs: have (possession), belong, resemble, suit, fit
→ "She has a car" cannot become passive.

🎯 Exam Tips & Common Traps

🎯 Exam Tip: Active → Passive Voice rules:

  • Object becomes Subject | Verb → "be + V3" | Subject → "by + object"
  • Present Continuous: is being + V3
  • Past Continuous: was being + V3
  • Present Perfect: has/have been + V3
  • Modal: modal + be + V3
  • No passive for: intransitive verbs (go, come, die, sleep)

Preposition Usage & Collocations

Correct preposition with specific verbs, adjectives, and nouns
⭐⭐ (11 PYQs)

Core Rule

Many verbs, adjectives, and nouns are followed by specific prepositions. Using the wrong preposition is a very common SSC error. These combinations must be memorized.

Verb + Preposition

✓
insist on | succeed in | believe in | rely on | depend on
✓
consist of | result in (cause) | result from (because of) | differ from
✓
die of (disease) | die from (injury) | die for (cause) | agree with (person) | agree to (plan)

Adjective + Preposition

✓
afraid of | fond of | proud of | aware of | capable of
✓
addicted to | averse to | devoted to | accustomed to
✓
good at | bad at | responsible for | famous for | angry with (person)

Common Mistakes

✗
He is afraid from dogs.
→ He is afraid of dogs.
✗
She succeeded to get the job.
→ She succeeded in getting the job.

🎯 Exam Tips & Common Traps

🎯 Exam Tip: Preposition errors are very common in SSC:

  • afraid of (not "from") | fond of | proud of
  • addicted to | averse to | keen on
  • rely on | depend on | insist on
  • succeed in | believe in | result in/from
  • differ from (things) | differ with (people)

Conjunctions & Connectors

Paired conjunctions and sentence connectors
⭐⭐ (11 PYQs)

Core Rule

Paired conjunctions (correlative conjunctions) must always be used in their correct pairs. Mixing up pairs is a common SSC error.

Paired Conjunctions

✓
Not only...but also | Either...or | Neither...nor
She is not only beautiful but also intelligent.
✓
Both...and (plural verb) | Whether...or
Both Ravi and Sita are coming.
✓
Hardly...when | Scarcely...when | No sooner...than
Hardly had she arrived when it rained. No sooner had he left than the phone rang.

Common Mistakes

✗
Hardly had she arrived than it rained.
→ Hardly...when (not "than"). No sooner...than (not "when").
✗
Although he is poor, but he is honest.
→ Use one, not both: Although he is poor, he is honest. OR He is poor but honest.

🎯 Exam Tips & Common Traps

🎯 Exam Tip: Paired conjunctions — keep the pair intact:

  • Not only...but also | Either...or | Neither...nor
  • No sooner...than | Hardly...when | Scarcely...when
  • Both...and | Whether...or
  • Don't mix pairs: "not only...but" ✗ → "not only...but also" ✓

Tense Usage & Sequence

Correct tense in context and sequence of tenses
⭐⭐ (23 PYQs)

Core Rule

The sequence of tenses rule: the tense in the subordinate clause must be consistent with the main clause. If the main clause is in past tense, the subordinate clause should also be in past (unless stating a universal truth).

Tense Quick Reference

→
Simple Present → Simple Past (after past reporting verb)
He said, "I play cricket." → He said he played cricket.
→
Past → Past Perfect (action completed before another past action)
He had left before I arrived. (left = first action)
✓
Universal truths stay in Present even after past reporting verb
The teacher said that the earth is round. (not "was round")

Common Mistakes

✗
When I will reach home, I will call you.
→ When I reach home, I will call you. (no "will" in time clauses)
✗
He said that he is tired.
→ He said that he was tired. (past → past)

🎯 Exam Tips & Common Traps

🎯 Exam Tip: Sequence of tenses — the tense in the subordinate clause must match the main clause:

  • Main clause in Past → subordinate clause in Past/Past Perfect
  • Universal truths stay in Present: He said that the earth is round
  • "Had + V3" for action completed before another past action

66

Article Usage (Comprehensive)

A, An, The — when to use and when to omit
⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ (266 PYQs)

Core Rule

Articles (a, an, the) come before nouns. Choose based on: countable/uncountable, singular/plural, specific/general. "A/An" = indefinite (any one). "The" = definite (specific one).

When to Use "A" / "An"

✓
Based on sound, not letter: a university (yoo) | an hour (silent h) | an MBA (em)
✓
Before singular countable noun (first mention): I saw a dog.

When to Use "The"

✓
Superlatives (the best), ordinals (the first), unique things (the sun)
✓
Rivers, oceans, mountain ranges, deserts: the Ganga, the Himalayas
✓
Adjective → class of people: The poor = poor people

No Article

✓
General uncountable/plural: Water is precious. Dogs are loyal.
✓
Languages, meals, games, subjects: I speak Hindi. I play cricket.

Common Mistakes

✗
He is an European.
→ He is a European. ("yoo" sound = consonant)
✗
I study the physics.
→ I study physics. (no article before subjects)

🎯 Exam Tips & Common Traps

🎯 Exam Tip: Article usage — one of the most tested topics:

  • "A/An" before consonant/vowel SOUND (not letter): a university (yoo sound), an hour (silent h)
  • "The" with unique things: the sun, the moon, the earth
  • No article with uncountable nouns used generally: water is precious
  • "The" with adjectives = plural noun: the poor = poor people

Subject-Verb Agreement (General)

Verb must agree with its subject in number and person
⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ (162 PYQs)

Core Rule

The verb must agree with its subject in number and person. Intervening phrases (with, along with, as well as, together with, besides, except) do NOT change the subject's number.

Key Agreement Rules

✓
Uncountable nouns = singular: news, information, advice, furniture, luggage, equipment
The news is true. (not "are") | This furniture is expensive.
✓
Plural-looking but singular: mathematics, physics, economics, politics, athletics
Mathematics is difficult. (not "are")
✓
Singular-looking but plural: people, police, cattle, clergy
The police are investigating. (not "is")
✓
There is/are — verb agrees with noun after it
There are many reasons. (reasons = plural)
✓
Collective nouns (team, committee, family) = singular (acting as one unit)
The team is playing well.

Common Mistakes

✗
The news are shocking.
→ The news is shocking. (uncountable = singular)
✗
The police is coming.
→ The police are coming. (always plural)

🎯 Exam Tips & Common Traps

🎯 Exam Tip: Subject-Verb Agreement — most tested grammar topic in SSC:

  • Intervening phrases don't affect verb: The book, along with notes, is here
  • "There is/are" — verb agrees with the noun after: There are many reasons
  • Collective nouns → singular verb (in Indian English): The team is playing
  • Uncountable nouns → singular verb: The news is true

Idioms & Phrases

Common English idioms and their meanings
— (1 PYQs)

Core Rule

An idiom is a fixed expression whose meaning cannot be understood from individual words. SSC exams test common English idioms — you must memorize them.

Most Tested Idioms

✓
A piece of cake = very easy | Break the ice = start conversation
✓
Burn the midnight oil = study/work late | Hit the nail on the head = exactly right
✓
Turn a blind eye = ignore | Beat around the bush = avoid main topic
✓
Under the weather = sick | Once in a blue moon = very rarely
✓
Kill two birds with one stone = achieve two things at once | Cost an arm and a leg = very expensive
✓
Let the cat out of the bag = reveal secret | Turn over a new leaf = fresh start

🎯 Exam Tips & Common Traps

🎯 Exam Tip: Learn these common idioms — they appear in every SSC exam:

  • A piece of cake = very easy
  • Break the ice = start a conversation
  • Burn the midnight oil = study/work late at night
  • Hit the nail on the head = be exactly right
  • Turn a blind eye = ignore deliberately
  • Beat around the bush = avoid the main topic

Commonly Confused Words

Words that sound alike or have similar meanings but differ in usage
— (2 PYQs)

Core Rule

Many English words look or sound similar but have different meanings. Using the wrong word changes the sentence's meaning. SSC frequently tests these pairs.

Most Tested Confused Pairs

✓
Affect (verb: influence) vs Effect (noun: result)
The rain affected the match. | The effect was visible.
✓
Accept (receive) vs Except (excluding)
I accept your offer. | Everyone came except him.
✓
Advice (noun) vs Advise (verb) | Principal (head) vs Principle (rule)
✓
Stationary (not moving) vs Stationery (writing materials)
✓
Complement (complete) vs Compliment (praise) | Fewer (countable) vs Less (uncountable)

🎯 Exam Tips & Common Traps

🎯 Exam Tip: Commonly confused word pairs:

  • Affect (verb: influence) vs Effect (noun: result)
  • Accept (receive) vs Except (excluding)
  • Advice (noun) vs Advise (verb)
  • Principal (head/main) vs Principle (rule/belief)
  • Stationary (not moving) vs Stationery (writing materials)

Word choice based on context and meaning

Core Rule

For vocabulary fill-in-the-blank questions: read the full sentence for context, identify the needed part of speech, eliminate wrong options, then choose the best fit.

Strategy

✓
Step1: Read the full sentence — understand context and tone
✓
Step2: Identify part of speech needed (noun/verb/adjective/adverb)
✓
Step3: Eliminate clearly wrong options, then pick the best contextual fit

🎯 Exam Tips & Common Traps

🎯 Exam Tip: For vocabulary questions:

  • Read the full sentence for context before choosing
  • Eliminate options that are clearly wrong first
  • Watch for words that sound similar but have different meanings
  • Check if the word fits grammatically (noun/verb/adjective/adverb)

71

Sentence Improvement

Identifying and correcting grammatical errors in sentences
⭐⭐⭐⭐ (84 PYQs)

Core Rule

In Sentence Improvement, a part is underlined. Check if it's correct or needs fixing. Look for: subject-verb agreement, tense, preposition, parallel structure, article usage, and word order.

What to Check

✓
1. Subject-Verb Agreement: The team are → The team is
✓
2. Tense: He said he is → He said he was
✓
3. Preposition: insisted for → insisted on
✓
4. Parallel structure: likes reading, to write → likes reading, writing
✓
5. Redundancy: returned back → returned

🎯 Exam Tips & Common Traps

🎯 Exam Tip: For sentence improvement questions:

  • Read the underlined part carefully — identify what type of error it might be
  • Check: subject-verb agreement, tense consistency, parallel structure
  • Check: correct preposition, article usage, word order
  • The correct option must be grammatically correct AND convey the intended meaning
📝
SSC CGL 15/09/2025 (Shift 1) 2025
She is junior than him in experience.
(a) junior from him
(b) more junior than him
(c) junior to him ✓
(d) younger to him
✅ Correct Answer: (c) junior to him
Explanation: (c) junior to him There are some words that imply comparison but do not take ‘than’. Rather, ‘to’ is used with them. For example:- superior to, inferior to, prior to, senior to, junior to, elder to, etc. Hence, “junior to him” is the most appropriate answer. (Correct)
📝
SSC CGL 15/09/2025 (Shift 1) 2025
He do not likes to be disturbed while studying.
(a) do not like
(b) does not liked
(c) does not like ✓
(d) is not liking
✅ Correct Answer: (c) does not like
Explanation: (c) does not like According to the “Subject-Verb Agreement Rule”, a singular subject always takes a singular verb and a plural subject always takes a plural verb. The subject ‘He’ is singular and therefore takes the singular helping verb ‘does’. Hence, “does not like” is the most appropriate answer....
📝
SSC CGL 16/09/2025 (Shift 2) 2025
He decided to marry with her despite his parents' objections.
(a) marry her
(b) marrying with her
(c) to marry to her
(d) to marry her ✓
✅ Correct Answer: (d) to marry her
Explanation: (d) to marry her When 'marry' is used as a transitive verb(with a direct object), it does not require a preposition like 'with' or 'to'. Therefore, ‘with’ must be removed. Hence, ‘to marry her’ is the most appropriate answer. (Correct)
📝

(a) tried harder to succeed
(b) try harder to succeed ✓
(c) tries hard to succeed
(d) should tried harder to succeed
✅ Correct Answer: (b) try harder to succeed
Explanation: (b) try harder to succeed After verbs like suggest, recommend, insist, demand, etc., we use the subjunctive mood, where the verb takes its base form (without -s). Hence, “try harder to succeed” is the most appropriate answer. (Correct)

(a) to learn swimming
(b) on learning swimming
(c) in learning to swim

Explanation: (d) on learning to swim ‘On’ is a fixed preposition used after the adjective ‘keen’ to indicate interest or enthusiasm about something. Hence, “on learning to swim” is the most appropriate answer. (Correct)

72

Spot the Error

Finding the part of a sentence that contains a grammatical error
⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ (232 PYQs)

Core Rule

In Spot the Error, a sentence is divided into parts (1), (2), (3), (4). Find which part has the grammatical error. If no error, answer is (4) "No error."

Most Common Error Types (by frequency)

→
1. Subject-Verb Agreement — most common
Each of the boys (1)/ are ready (2)/ for the exam. → (2) "are" should be "is"
→
2. Tense Errors
When I will reach (1)/ home, I will call you. → (1) "will reach" should be "reach"
→
3. Preposition Errors
He is addicted (1)/ for smoking (2)/ since childhood. → (2) "for" should be "to"
→
4. Article Errors
He is (1)/ an European (2)/ by birth. → (2) "an" should be "a"
→
5. Pronoun Errors
Everyone should (1)/ do their duty (2)/ honestly. → (2) "their" should be "his"

🎯 Exam Tips & Common Traps

🎯 Exam Tip: For spot-the-error questions:

  • Read each part (1), (2), (3), (4) separately
  • Check each part for: subject-verb agreement, tense, preposition, article
  • If you can't find the error, the answer is "No error" (4)
  • Most errors are in: verb form, preposition, article, or pronoun agreement

Pinnacle Practice Set 2025
Can you please / pass me that / glittery pen black?
(a) pass me that
(b) glittery pen black? ✓
(c) Can you please
(d) No error
✅ Correct Answer: (b) glittery pen black?
Explanation: (b) glittery pen black? Adjectives should be written before the noun (pen) that is being qualified. The general order of adjectives before a noun is the following: Opinion, Size, Shape, Condition, Age, Colour,Pattern, Origin, Material and Purpose. ‘Glittery’ represents opinion and ‘black’ is the color. Hence, ‘glittery black pen’ is the most appropriate answer. (Correct)
